title: Χύτραι
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 354. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Χύτραν ὀστρακίνην καὶ χαλκῆν ποταμὸς κατέφερεν.
sentences.tr: Chytran ostrakinēn kai chalkēn potamos katepheren.
sentences.l: An earthenware pot and a bronze one a river was carrying down.
sentences.i: A river was sweeping along an earthenware pot and a bronze one.
sentences.n: The noun χύτραν stands once and carries both adjectives — Greek says 'an earthen and a bronze pot' where English needs the noun twice. The title, by contrast, has the plural Χύτραι.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ὀστρακίνη τῇ χαλκῇ ἔλεγεν· « Μακρόθεν μου κολύμβα, καὶ μὴ πλησίον· ἐὰν γάρ μοι σὺ προσψαύσῃς, κατακλῶμαι, κἂν ἐγὼ μὴ θέλουσα προσψαύσω. »
sentences.tr: Hē de ostrakinē tēi chalkēi elegen· « Makrothen mou kolymba, kai mē plēsion· ean gar moi sy prospsausēis, kataklōmai, kan egō mē thelousa prospsausō. »
sentences.l: And the earthen one was saying to the bronze one: « Swim far off from me, and not near; for if you touch me, I am broken in pieces, and if I, not wishing it, should touch you. »
sentences.i: And the earthen pot said to the bronze one: « Swim well away from me, and not close; for if you touch me I am smashed — and just as much if I touch you, however little I mean to. »
sentences.n: κἄν is καὶ ἐάν run together by crasis, with the aorist subjunctive προσψαύσω following it as with the plain ἐάν above. μή negates the participle θέλουσα because the whole clause is a supposition, not a statement of fact. The present κατακλῶμαι is not 'I am being broken' but the general truth: that is simply what happens to me.

sentences.t: Ὅτι ἐπισφαλής ἐστι βίος πένητι δυναστοῦ ἅρπαγος πλησίον παροικοῦντι.
sentences.tr: Hoti episphalēs esti bios penēti dynastou harpagos plēsion paroikounti.
sentences.l: That life is precarious for a poor man dwelling near a rapacious lord.
sentences.i: The story shows that life is precarious for a poor man who lives near a rapacious lord.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. πλησίον, 'near', takes the genitive (δυναστοῦ ἅρπαγος), while παροικοῦντι agrees with πένητι. ἐπισφαλής is what is liable to trip and fall — a footing that will not hold.
